title: Percentage
summary: The language of the whole arithmetic section — profit-loss, interest, discount and DI are all percentage questions in disguise. Tier 1 asks 1–2 direct questions per shift (successive change, more/less flips, election and population problems) and Tier 2 leans on it heavily.

subtopics.title: Percentage meaning & conversions
subtopics.concept:
Per cent means 'out of every hundred'. So $25\%$ means 25 parts out of every 100 parts, which is the same as $\dfrac{1}{4}$.

Every percentage is just a fraction. Turn the percent into a fraction first, and the question becomes plain arithmetic.

formulas.name: x% of a number
formulas.note: Turn the percent into a fraction first; cancel where you can.

formulas.name: Whole from a part
formulas.note: x is the percent that the part stands for.

formulas.name: A as a percent of B
formulas.note: B is the quantity that follows the word 'of'.

formulas.name: Remaining part
formulas.note: Only when both percentages are of the same whole.

tricks.title: Let the fraction table do the division
tricks.body: Replace the percent with its fraction from the table. $12.5\%$ becomes $\dfrac{1}{8}$, so the sum turns into a simple division.

example.q: What is 12.5% of 960?

tricks.title: Build the percent from 10% and 1% pieces
tricks.body: Move the decimal point for $10\%$ and $1\%$, then add pieces. Works without pen-and-paper multiplication.

example.q: What is 24% of 650?

tricks.title: Swap x% of y into y% of x
tricks.body: $x\%$ of $y$ always equals $y\%$ of $x$. Swap when one side turns into a friendly percent.

example.q: What is 4% of 25?

mistakes.wrong: In 'A is what per cent of B', putting A below the line.
mistakes.right: The quantity after 'of' is the base: $A \div B \times 100$.

mistakes.wrong: Treating $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ as roughly $16.3\%$.
mistakes.right: It is exactly $\dfrac{1}{6}$. Use the fraction from the table.

mistakes.wrong: Turning a fraction into a percent by dividing by 100.
mistakes.right: Multiply by 100: $1/4$ becomes $25\%$.

mistakes.wrong: Reading $0.5\%$ as $5\%$.
mistakes.right: $0.5\%$ is half of one per cent, that is $\dfrac{1}{200}$ of the number.

mistakes.wrong: Adding percents of different wholes in one line.
mistakes.right: Percents add only when they are percents of the same whole.

mistakes.wrong: Finding the whole by multiplying the part by the percent.
mistakes.right: Divide instead: whole $=$ part $\times 100 \div$ percent.

subtopics.notes:
### What per cent means
Per cent means "out of every hundred". $40\%$ means 40 parts taken out of every 100 parts.

- $40\% = \dfrac{40}{100} = \dfrac{2}{5}$
- $50\%$ is half, $100\%$ is the whole thing
- $200\%$ is double

> **Rule:** Before any calculation, write the percent as a fraction with 100 below. Then cancel.

### The fraction table
Exams reuse the same fractions again and again. Learn this table by heart; it saves a multiplication in almost every question.

| Fraction | Percent | | Fraction | Percent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1/2$ | 50% | | $1/8$ | 12.5% |
| $1/3$ | 33 1/3% | | $1/9$ | 11 1/9% |
| $1/4$ | 25% | | $1/11$ | 9 1/11% |
| $1/5$ | 20% | | $1/12$ | 8 1/3% |
| $1/6$ | 16 2/3% | | $1/15$ | 6 2/3% |
| $1/7$ | 14 2/7% | | $1/16$ | 6.25% |
| $1/20$ | 5% | | $1/25$ | 4% |

Half the table comes free: $1/6$ is half of $1/3$, so $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ is half of $33\dfrac{1}{3}\%$.

- Fraction to percent: multiply by 100. $\dfrac{5}{16} \times 100 = 31.25\%$.
- Percent to fraction: put over 100 and cancel. $12.5\% = \dfrac{125}{1000} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

### Finding a percentage of a number
$x\%$ of $N$ means $\dfrac{x}{100} \times N$.

$35\%$ of $200 = \dfrac{35}{100} \times 200 = 70$.

Use the table when the percent is in it. $12.5\%$ is $\dfrac{1}{8}$, so $12.5\%$ of $960 = 960 \div 8 = 120$. No big multiplication needed.

> **Example:** $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ of $720$: the percent is $\dfrac{1}{6}$, so the answer is $720 \div 6 = 120$.

### The 10% and 1% building blocks
Split an awkward percent into pieces of $10\%$ and $1\%$.

1. $10\%$ of a number: move the decimal point one place left.
2. $1\%$ of a number: move it two places left.
3. Add pieces until you build the percent you need.

$24\%$ of $650$: two $10\%$ pieces give $130$, four $1\%$ pieces give $26$, total $156$.

> **Tip:** $x\%$ of $y$ always equals $y\%$ of $x$. So $4\%$ of $25$ equals $25\%$ of $4$, which is clearly $1$.

### Finding the whole from a part
Here the question gives a piece of a number and its percent. The full number is asked.

> **Rule:** whole $=$ part $\times\ 100 \div$ percent.

$35\%$ of a number is $189$. So the number is $189 \times \dfrac{100}{35} = 540$. Then $80\%$ of it is $\dfrac{4}{5} \times 540 = 432$.

Sanity check: the whole (540) must be bigger than the part (189), because $35\%$ is less than the whole.

### One quantity as a percentage of another
"A is what per cent of B?" means $\dfrac{A}{B} \times 100$. The quantity after "of" goes below the line.

In a batch of 720 applications, 126 were rejected. Rejected applications are $\dfrac{126}{720} \times 100 = 17.5\%$ of the batch.

> **Watch:** The number after "of" is the base. Swap the two numbers and the answer changes.

### The remaining part of a hundred
Percentages of the same whole add up to $100\%$.

Out of 240 students, $62.5\%$ attended a function. So $37.5\%$ were absent, and $37.5\% = \dfrac{3}{8}$. Absent students $= \dfrac{3}{8} \times 240 = 90$.

> **Note:** Equal-percent statements also link two wholes. If $40\%$ of A $= 30\%$ of B, then $0.4A = 0.3B$, so $A = 75\%$ of B.

patterns.name: Find x% of a number
patterns.howToSpot: A number is given and a percentage of it is asked: 'What is 24% of 650?'
steps: Turn the percent into a fraction over 100.
Cancel it to a table fraction when possible.
Check size: the answer should look like a fraction of the number.
patterns.why: A percent is only a fraction, so taking a percent means taking that fraction of the number.

example.q: What is 24% of 650?

patterns.name: Find the number when a percent of it is given
patterns.howToSpot: '35% of a number is 189.' The number itself, or a second percent of it, is asked.
steps: Use this whole for any follow-up asked.
patterns.why: The part is a known fraction of the whole, so dividing by that fraction recovers the whole.

example.q: 35% of a number is 189. What is 80% of that number?

patterns.name: Change a fraction into a percentage
patterns.howToSpot: 'Express 5/16 as a percentage', or options are all in percent.
steps: Write the result as a decimal or mixed number.
patterns.why: Percent is a fraction with 100 below, so scaling the fraction to 100 gives the percent.

example.q: Express $\dfrac{5}{16}$ as a percentage.

patterns.name: One quantity as a percentage of another
patterns.howToSpot: '126 out of 720 applications were rejected.' What percentage one quantity is of another is asked.
steps: Put the quantity being asked about on top.
Put the total, the quantity after 'of', below.
patterns.why: The percent says how many per hundred the top quantity is of the bottom one.

example.q: In a batch of 720 applications, 126 were rejected. What percentage of the applications was rejected?

patterns.name: The remaining percentage
patterns.howToSpot: A part is described by a percent and the rest is asked: '62.5% attended. How many were absent?'
steps: Turn the remainder into a table fraction.
patterns.why: The two parts split the same total, so their percents add to 100.

example.q: Out of 240 students, 62.5% attended the annual function. How many students did not attend?

patterns.name: Equal percent statements
patterns.howToSpot: 'If 40% of A equals 30% of B...' Two different wholes are joined by one equation.
steps: Drop the percents and write the equation: 0.4A = 0.3B.
Solve for the ratio A over B.
Turn the ratio into a percent.
patterns.why: Two equal products fix the ratio of A and B, so one percent of the other follows.

example.q: If 40% of A is equal to 30% of B, then A is what percentage of B?

revision: Per cent means out of every hundred: $x\% = \dfrac{x}{100}$.
A as a per cent of B: $A \div B \times 100$; the number after 'of' stays below.
Percents of the same whole add to $100\%$.

subtopics.title: Percentage increase / decrease & successive change
subtopics.concept:
A percentage change compares a new value with an old value. The **old** value is always the base, so it stays below the line.

The fast method: turn each change into a **multiplier**. $+20\%$ means $\times \dfrac{6}{5}$, $-10\%$ means $\times \dfrac{9}{10}$. Chain changes by multiplying multipliers.

formulas.name: Multiplier
formulas.note: Plus for a rise, minus for a fall.

formulas.name: Successive changes
formulas.note: a and b carry their own signs.

formulas.name: Same x% up and down
formulas.note: x% rise followed by x% cut.

tricks.title: One multiplication per change
tricks.body: Replace every rise or fall with its multiplier fraction and multiply once. This replaces three lines of working.

example.q: A price fell by 12.5% to Rs 3,500. What was the price before the fall?

tricks.title: a + b + ab/100 for two changes
tricks.body: Two changes in a row combine by this one formula. Keep the signs of both percents.

example.q: A value rises by 15% and then by 12%. What is the net percentage change?

tricks.title: Round trip loses x squared over 100
tricks.body: A rise of x% followed by a cut of x% always ends below the start, by exactly $\dfrac{x^2}{100}$ per cent.

example.q: A price is raised by 20% and then reduced by 20%. What is the net change?

mistakes.wrong: Adding percents of different bases: $20\%$ up then $10\%$ down called $10\%$ up.
mistakes.right: Combine with multipliers or $a + b + \dfrac{ab}{100}$ with signs.

mistakes.wrong: Measuring change against the new value.
mistakes.right: The old value is the base. Divide the difference by the old value.

mistakes.wrong: Undoing a $20\%$ rise by subtracting $20\%$.
mistakes.right: Divide by the multiplier: $\text{new} \div 1.2$.

mistakes.wrong: Undoing a fall with the wrong chip, e.g. $\times 0.9$ for a $10\%$ fall.
mistakes.right: A fall used $9/10$; undo it with $\times \dfrac{10}{9}$.

mistakes.wrong: Calling an up-then-down round trip 'no change'.
mistakes.right: It always loses $\dfrac{x^2}{100}$ per cent.

mistakes.wrong: Applying $+10\%$ twice and calling it $+20\%$.

subtopics.notes:
### Change is measured against the old value
Per cent change $= \dfrac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \times 100$. The old value sits below the line.

A shop's sales rose from 18,000 to 20,700. Change $= 2700$, and $\dfrac{2700}{18000} \times 100 = 15\%$.

> **Rule:** Old value below, always. Ask yourself "which number came first?" before dividing.

> **Watch:** 250 growing to 300 is $+20\%$, but 200 growing to 250 is $+25\%$. The same 50 gives different percents because the bases differ.

### Multipliers: the fastest method
Do not add and subtract in steps. Multiply by one fraction per change.

| Change | Multiplier | | Change | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $+10\%$ | $11/10$ | | $-10\%$ | $9/10$ |
| $+20\%$ | $6/5$ | | $-20\%$ | $4/5$ |
| $+25\%$ | $5/4$ | | $-25\%$ | $3/4$ |
| $+50\%$ | $3/2$ | | $-50\%$ | $1/2$ |

$18000 \times \dfrac{23}{20} = 20700$: a $15\%$ rise in one multiplication, and $+15\%$ or $-15\%$ both come from the chips $23/20$ and $17/20$.

To undo a change, divide by the same multiplier. $-20\%$ turned 50,000 into 40,000, so $40000 \div \dfrac{4}{5} = 50000$.

### Two changes one after the other
Multiply the two multipliers, or use one formula.

$$\text{net change} = a + b + \frac{ab}{100}$$

Here $a$ and $b$ carry their own signs. $+15\%$ then $+12\%$: $15 + 12 + \dfrac{15 \times 12}{100} = 28.8\%$, a rise.

With multipliers: $\dfrac{23}{20} \times \dfrac{28}{25} = \dfrac{161}{125} = 1.288$, the same $+28.8\%$.

$+20\%$ then $-10\%$: $\dfrac{6}{5} \times \dfrac{9}{10} = \dfrac{27}{25}$, a net rise of $8\%$.

> **Careful:** Never just add the percents. $20\%$ up and $10\%$ down is not $10\%$ up.

### The round trip: x% up then x% down
Raise a value by $x\%$ and then cut it by $x\%$. It does not come back.

$$\text{net loss} = \left(\frac{x}{10}\right)^2 \%$$

$10\%$ up then $10\%$ down: $\dfrac{11}{10} \times \dfrac{9}{10} = \dfrac{99}{100}$, a $1\%$ loss.
$20\%$ up then $20\%$ down: $\dfrac{6}{5} \times \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{24}{25}$, a $4\%$ loss.

> **Note:** The order does not matter. Up first or down first, the loss is the same $x^2/100$ per cent.

### Getting the original back
If a value fell or rose and the final value is given, divide by the multiplier to undo the change.

A number became 8,100 after two yearly falls of $10\%$. Two chips of $9/10$ were used, so the original $= 8100 \times \dfrac{10}{9} \times \dfrac{10}{9} = 10000$.

A number is decreased by $10\%$, then by $20\%$, and becomes 720. Original $= 720 \times \dfrac{10}{9} \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 1000$.

> **Watch:** To undo $+20\%$, divide by $1.2$. Subtracting $20\%$ back is wrong.

### When the top and bottom of a fraction change
A fraction's value changes by the top's chip divided by the bottom's chip.

The numerator rises $50\%$ (chip $3/2$) and the denominator falls $25\%$ (chip $3/4$):
$$\text{new value} = \text{old} \times \frac{3/2}{3/4} = \text{old} \times 2$$
The fraction doubles.

> **Example:** Numerator $+20\%$ (chip $6/5$), denominator $-10\%$ (chip $9/10$): value $ \times \dfrac{6/5}{9/10} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, a $33\dfrac{1}{3}\%$ rise.

patterns.name: Percentage increase or decrease
patterns.howToSpot: Two values of the same thing are given and the per cent change is asked.
steps: Find the difference between the new and old values.
Multiply by 100 and attach increase or decrease.
patterns.why: Per cent change states the difference as a part of the starting value.

example.q: A shop's monthly sales rose from Rs 18,000 to Rs 20,700. What was the percentage increase?

patterns.name: Two successive changes
patterns.howToSpot: A value changes twice in a row and the net change is asked: '+20% and then -10%'.
steps: Write both percents with their signs.
Add them and add ab/100 as well.
State rise or fall from the sign.
Cross-check by multiplying the two multipliers.
patterns.why: The second change acts on the changed value, so a small cross term ab/100 appears.

example.q: A number is increased by 20% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net percentage change?

patterns.name: Same x% up and then down
patterns.howToSpot: A value rises by x% and falls by the same x%; the net effect is asked.
steps: State it as a net loss.
patterns.why: The two chips multiply to $1 - \dfrac{x^2}{10000}$, always a shade below 1.

example.q: The price of an article is raised by 20% and then reduced by 20%. What is the net change in price?

patterns.name: Find the original value
patterns.howToSpot: A value after some change is given and the value before the change is asked.
steps: Write the multiplier for each change that happened.
Divide the final value by the product of the multipliers.
Check by applying the changes to your answer.
patterns.why: Changes were multiplications, so undoing them is division by the same multipliers.

example.q: A number is first decreased by 10% and then decreased by 20%. The result is 720. What was the original number?

patterns.name: Numerator and denominator both change
patterns.howToSpot: A fraction's top and bottom are each changed by a percent and the effect on the fraction is asked.
steps: Write the chip for the numerator's change.
Write the chip for the denominator's change.
Multiply the old fraction by top chip over bottom chip.
patterns.why: The top scales the fraction up and the bottom scales it down, so the chips divide.

example.q: In a fraction the numerator is increased by 50% and the denominator is decreased by 25%. The new fraction is how many times the old one?

patterns.name: Three or more successive changes
patterns.howToSpot: Three changes are applied one after another and the net effect is asked.
steps: Write a multiplier for each change.
Compare the product with 1 to get the net per cent.
patterns.why: Multipliers keep working for any number of changes; only the multiplication grows.

example.q: A value is increased by 10%, then increased by 20%, and then decreased by 25%. What is the net percentage change?

revision: Two changes: multiply the multipliers, or $a + b + \dfrac{ab}{100}$.
Undo a change by dividing by the same multiplier.
Fraction value $\times$ top chip $\div$ bottom chip.

subtopics.title: 'x% more than' ↔ 'x% less than' & chains
subtopics.concept:
'A is $25\%$ more than B' compares A with B, so B is the base. Said the other way round, B is compared with A, and the answer is different: B is $20\%$ less than A.

This subtopic is about flipping such statements both ways, quickly and correctly.

formulas.name: x% more, reversed
formulas.note: x% more than becomes this much less than.

formulas.name: x% less, reversed
formulas.note: x% less than becomes this much more than.

formulas.name: Per cent of a per cent

tricks.title: Memorise the standard pairs
tricks.body: Four pairs cover most papers: 25/20, 20/$16\dfrac{2}{3}$, 50/$33\dfrac{1}{3}$, and 100/50. Read the question, write the partner, done.

example.q: If A's income is 20% less than B's, then B's income is more than A's by:

tricks.title: Base-100 when memory fails
tricks.body: Put the base quantity at 100, write the other quantity, and divide by the new base. Slow but never wrong.

example.q: A's salary is 60% more than B's. B's salary is less than A's by what percentage?

tricks.title: Awkward percents: use the fraction
tricks.body: $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ is $1/6$, so 'more by $1/6$' reverses to 'less by $1/7$' of the bigger number.

example.q: X is 16 2/3% more than Y. By what percentage is Y less than X?

mistakes.wrong: Answering '$25\%$ less' for the reverse of '$25\%$ more'.
mistakes.right: The reverse is $\dfrac{100 \times 25}{125} = 20\%$ less.

mistakes.wrong: Writing 'A is $25\%$ more than B' as $A = B - 25\%$ of B.
mistakes.right: More means add: $A = B + \dfrac{25}{100}B = \dfrac{5}{4}B$.

mistakes.wrong: Using $100 + x$ in the less-to-more formula.
mistakes.right: Less-to-more divides by $100 - x$; more-to-less divides by $100 + x$.

mistakes.wrong: Adding chained percents: $40\%$ and $25\%$ of them called $65\%$.
mistakes.right: Multiply instead: $25\%$ of $40\% = 10\%$.

mistakes.wrong: Calling $75\%$ less the reverse of $75\%$ more.
mistakes.right: $75\%$ less reverses to $\dfrac{100 \times 75}{25} = 300\%$ more.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding $14\dfrac{2}{7}\%$ to $14.2\%$ and losing the fraction.
mistakes.right: Keep sevenths as fractions; the options use $14\dfrac{2}{7}$.

subtopics.notes:
### The base decides the answer
Take "A is $25\%$ more than B". Put B at 100, so A is 125.

Now read it backwards: B is less than A by $25$ out of $125$, and $\dfrac{25}{125} \times 100 = 20\%$. So B is $20\%$ less than A.

Same pair, two different percents. The base changed.

> **Rule:** The quantity after "than" is the base. Flip the statement and the base flips too.

### The two flip formulas
You do not need to test with 100 every time.

$$x\% \text{ more} \Rightarrow \frac{100x}{100+x}\% \text{ less}$$
$$x\% \text{ less} \Rightarrow \frac{100x}{100-x}\% \text{ more}$$

Check with 25: $25\%$ more becomes $\dfrac{100 \times 25}{125} = 20\%$ less. And $20\%$ less becomes $\dfrac{100 \times 20}{80} = 25\%$ more.

> **Watch:** $25\%$ more and $25\%$ less are not a matching pair. Their partners are $20\%$ less and $33\dfrac{1}{3}\%$ more.

### Set the base to 100
When unsure, do not trust memory of formulas. Build the numbers.

"A's salary is $60\%$ more than B's." B $= 100$, A $= 160$. B is less by $\dfrac{60}{160}$ of A, and $\dfrac{60}{160} \times 100 = 37.5\%$.

> **Example:** A town's population fell from 1,500 to 1,200. The rise needed to get back: $\dfrac{300}{1200} \times 100 = 25\%$. The fall was only $\dfrac{300}{1500} = 20\%$.

### Pairs worth memorising
The same pairs appear every year. Learn the table and skip the working.

| Statement | Reverse |
|---|---|
| $25\%$ more | $20\%$ less |
| $20\%$ more | $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ less |
| $50\%$ more | $33\dfrac{1}{3}\%$ less |
| $100\%$ more | $50\%$ less |
| $25\%$ less | $33\dfrac{1}{3}\%$ more |
| $20\%$ less | $25\%$ more |
| $75\%$ less | $300\%$ more |

> **Tip:** Every pair multiplies back to itself. Undoing a change is the flip question in disguise.

### Chains of percentages
"A $40\%$ of B" language means multiply.

" $40\%$ of the candidates are graduates, and $25\%$ of the graduates are engineers." Engineers $= \dfrac{25}{100} \times \dfrac{40}{100} = \dfrac{1}{10} = 10\%$ of all candidates.

> **Note:** Each "of" starts from the group named just before it, not from the total.

### Awkward percents through fractions
Third-sixths and sevenths flip best as fractions.

$16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ more means $\times \dfrac{7}{6}$. Reversed, that is less by $\dfrac{1}{7}$, and $\dfrac{1}{7} \times 100 = 14\dfrac{2}{7}\%$.

"X is $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ more than Y" and "Y is $14\dfrac{2}{7}\%$ less than X" are the same fact.

> **Careful:** $14\dfrac{2}{7}\%$ is exact, not approximately 14.2. Keep it as the fraction $1/7$.

patterns.name: Convert 'x% more' into 'less'
patterns.howToSpot: 'A is some percent more than B. B is less than A by what percent?'
steps: Note x, the percent by which A beats B.
State it as the per cent by which B is less.
patterns.why: The same gap measured on the bigger base A gives a smaller percent.

example.q: A's salary is 60% more than B's. B's salary is less than A's by what percentage?

patterns.name: Convert 'x% less' into 'more'
patterns.howToSpot: 'A is some percent less than B. B is more than A by what percent?'
steps: Note x, the percent of the fall.
State it as the per cent by which B is more.
patterns.why: The same gap measured on the smaller base A gives a bigger percent.

example.q: A's income is 20% less than B's. B's income is more than A's by what percentage?

patterns.name: Per cent of a per cent
patterns.howToSpot: One group is a percent of a second group, which is itself a percent of a total.
steps: Attach each percent to its own group.
Multiply the two percents as fractions.
Simplify to a single percent of the total.
patterns.why: Every 'of' multiplies, so a percent of a percent is a product.

example.q: In an examination centre, 40% of the candidates are graduates, and 25% of the graduates are engineers. Engineers are what percentage of all candidates?

patterns.name: Two quantities on a common base
patterns.howToSpot: Two quantities are each compared with the same third quantity, and then with each other.
steps: Put the shared base quantity at 100.
Write both quantities from the two statements.
Take the ratio of the two quantities.
patterns.why: A common base makes the two quantities comparable in one ratio.

example.q: X is 50% more than Z, and Y is 20% more than Z. Y is what percentage of X?

patterns.name: Awkward percents through fractions
patterns.howToSpot: Percents like $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ or $14\dfrac{2}{7}\%$ appear, and a flip is asked.
steps: Write the percent as a fraction from the table.
Add or subtract that fraction from 1 for the bigger quantity.
The leftover fraction, over the bigger quantity, is the reverse percent.
patterns.why: Fraction chips reverse exactly, with no division of awkward decimals.

example.q: X is $16\dfrac{2}{3}\%$ more than Y. By what percentage is Y less than X?

revision: Base-100 always works: put the 'than' quantity at 100.
Each 'of' in a chain multiplies: $a\%$ of $b\% = ab/10000$.

subtopics.title: Population growth, depreciation & elections
subtopics.concept:
Population and machine-value questions apply a per cent change **every year**, so the change compounds. Election questions first remove invalid votes, then compare candidates on valid votes.

Both are multiplier questions wearing a story.

formulas.name: Depreciation for n years
formulas.note: r% of value lost every year.

formulas.name: Value n years ago
formulas.note: Divide by the chip power to go back.

tricks.title: Chip powers beat formulas
tricks.body: Write one multiplier per year and multiply. Squares like $\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{25}{16}$ are worth remembering.

example.q: A town of 6,400 people grows by 25% every year. What is its population after 2 years?

tricks.title: Remove invalid votes first
tricks.body: In elections, bring every statement onto valid votes before touching the margin.

example.q: In an election, 20% of the votes polled were invalid. The winner secured 60% of the valid votes and beat the only other candidate by 1,200 votes. How many votes were polled?

tricks.title: Roll, cast, valid: walk the chain
tricks.body: Election numbers form a chain: roll, votes cast, valid votes, then candidates. Convert one link at a time with chips.

example.q: In an election, 20% of the voters on the roll did not vote. The winner got 55% of the votes cast and won by 1,200 votes. How many voters were on the roll?

mistakes.wrong: Using simple growth $P + Prn$ for population.
mistakes.right: Population compounds: $P \times \left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^n$.

mistakes.wrong: Taking every year's depreciation on the original value.
mistakes.right: Each year falls on that year's value, so multiply chips.

mistakes.wrong: Applying the chip $n-1$ times for $n$ years.
mistakes.right: Count on fingers: 2 years means the chip twice.

mistakes.wrong: Computing candidate percents on total votes polled.
mistakes.right: Remove invalid votes first; percents are on valid votes.

mistakes.wrong: Taking the winner's margin as a percent of the roll.
mistakes.right: The margin is the difference of two percents of valid or cast votes.

mistakes.wrong: Multiplying by the growth chip to find a past value.
mistakes.right: Going back divides by the chip, or multiplies by its inverse.

subtopics.notes:
### One rate, many years
A town grows by $r\%$ every year. Each year's population is the previous year's times the chip $\dfrac{100+r}{100}$.

$$\text{After } n \text{ years} = P \times \left(\frac{100+r}{100}\right)^n$$

A town of 50,000 grows $10\%$ a year. After 2 years: $50000 \times \dfrac{11}{10} \times \dfrac{11}{10} = 60500$.

> **Rule:** Growth per year compounds. Never use $P + P \times r \times n$, which is simple interest thinking.

### Different rates in different years
When each year has its own rate, multiply one chip per year in order.

A town of 40,000 grows $10\%$ one year and falls $5\%$ the next: $40000 \times \dfrac{11}{10} \times \dfrac{19}{20} = 41800$.

Three rates work the same way. A value that rose $20\%$, then $25\%$, then $10\%$ is now $66,000$; before those years it was $66000 \div \dfrac{33}{20} = 40000$.

> **Note:** $+10\%$ then $-5\%$ is not $+5\%$. The chips multiply, they do not cancel.

### Travelling back in time
To find an earlier value, divide by the chips.

A town has 16,000 people now and grows $25\%$ yearly. Two years ago: $16000 \div \dfrac{5}{4} \div \dfrac{5}{4} = 16000 \times \dfrac{16}{25} = 10240$.

> **Tip:** Dividing by $\dfrac{5}{4}$ twice is multiplying by $\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^2$. Reverse the chip, then square it.

### Depreciation compounds too
A machine loses value every year. That is a fall applied to the falling value, so it compounds.

A machine worth Rs 12,500 loses $10\%$ a year. After 2 years: $12500 \times \left(\dfrac{9}{10}\right)^2 = 10125$.

Running backwards: a machine is worth 8,100 after two years of $10\%$ yearly loss. It cost $8100 \times \left(\dfrac{10}{9}\right)^2 = 10000$.

> **Watch:** Each year's fall is taken on that year's value, never on the original price.

A rise of $25\%$ followed by a fall of $20\%$ does come back: $\dfrac{5}{4} \times \dfrac{4}{5} = 1$. But $+25\%$ then $-25\%$ leaves $\dfrac{5}{4} \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{15}{16}$, a loss.

### Elections: valid votes first
Votes polled $=$ valid votes $+$ invalid votes. Candidate percents are always on **valid** votes.

Worked: $20\%$ of votes polled were invalid. The winner got $60\%$ of valid votes and beat the only rival by 1,200 votes.

1. Two candidates, so the rival got $40\%$ of valid votes.
2. Margin $= 20\%$ of valid votes $= 1200$, so valid $= 6000$.
3. Polled $=$ valid $\times \dfrac{100}{80} = 6000 \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 7500$.

> **Careful:** "Votes polled" is not "valid votes". Remove the invalid share first.

### Voters who did not turn up
The electoral roll lists everyone. Votes cast $=$ roll $-$ those who did not vote.

Worked: $20\%$ of the roll did not vote. The winner got $55\%$ of votes cast and won by 1,200 votes.

1. Margin $= 55\% - 45\% = 10\%$ of votes cast $= 1200$, so cast $= 12000$.
2. Cast is $80\%$ of the roll, so roll $= 12000 \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 15000$.

> **Example:** 27,000 votes were polled in another ward and $10\%$ were invalid. Valid votes $= 27000 - 2700 = 24300$.

subtopics.title: Marks, income–expenditure–savings & price–consumption
subtopics.concept: Pass-marks questions hide one unknown: the **maximum marks**. Two candidates' scores pin it down. Income questions split money into expenditure and savings. Price questions link a price change to how much you can buy.

formulas.name: Maximum marks (two candidates)
formulas.note: a = shortfall below pass, b = marks above pass, x and y are the two percents.

formulas.name: Consumption cut after a price rise
Extra quantity after a price cut

tricks.title: Span of marks over span of percents
tricks.body: Two candidates give one clean fraction: marks apart over percents apart. Multiply by 100 for maximum marks.

example.q: In an examination, A scores 33% and fails by 45 marks. B scores 45% and gets 15 marks more than the pass mark. Find the maximum marks.

tricks.title: Price rise to consumption cut is a flip
tricks.body: Reuse the more/less flip: price up $x\%$ with the same budget means consumption down $\dfrac{100x}{100+x}\%$.

example.q: The price of petrol rises by 25%. By what per cent must a family cut its consumption to keep its spending the same?

tricks.title: Extra kilograms reveal the price
tricks.body: After a price cut, extra kilograms equal money times the difference of the chips, divided by the new price. Solve for the price.

example.q: Rs 400 is spent on rice. After a 20% fall in price, the same money buys 5 kg more. What was the original price per kg?
steps: Quantity chip $= \dfrac{5}{4}$, so extra $= \dfrac{1}{4}$ of old quantity.
Old quantity $= 20$ kg, so extra $= 5$ kg matches.

mistakes.wrong: Dividing by $(y - x)$ but forgetting to add $b$ to $a$.
mistakes.right: The marks span is the whole distance, shortfall plus surplus: $a + b$.

mistakes.wrong: Writing pass mark $= x\%$ of $M - a$ for a failing candidate.
mistakes.right: Failing means below pass: pass $= \dfrac{x}{100}M + a$.

mistakes.wrong: Measuring the savings change on the new savings.
mistakes.right: Per cent change uses the old value as the base.

mistakes.wrong: Cutting consumption by the same per cent as the price rise.
mistakes.right: Price up $25\%$ needs only a $20\%$ cut: $\dfrac{100x}{100+x}$.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the extra quantity per cent equal to the price cut.
mistakes.right: A $20\%$ cut buys $\dfrac{100 \times 20}{80} = 25\%$ more.

mistakes.wrong: Taking income as 100 but expenditure as a real rupee figure.
mistakes.right: Keep every number in the same units, assumed or real.

subtopics.notes:
### Pass marks with two candidates
One candidate scores $x\%$ and fails by $a$ marks. Another scores $y\%$ and gets $b$ marks more than the pass mark.

The gap between their scores covers $(y - x)\%$ of the maximum marks and equals $a + b$ marks.

$$M = \frac{(a + b) \times 100}{y - x}$$

Worked: A scores $33\%$ and fails by 45 marks. B scores $45\%$ and gets 15 marks more than the pass mark.

1. Span of percents $= 45 - 33 = 12$.
2. Span of marks $= 45 + 15 = 60$.
3. $M = 60 \times \dfrac{100}{12} = 500$.
4. Pass mark $= 33\%$ of $500 + 45 = 165 + 45 = 210$.

> **Rule:** One candidate sits below the pass mark, the other above. The whole distance is $a + b$.

### Pass marks with one candidate
"Fails by $a$" means the score plus $a$ equals the pass mark.

A student scores $30\%$ and fails by 20 marks; the pass mark is 152. Then $30\%$ of $M = 152 - 20 = 132$, so $M = 440$.

> **Tip:** Write "$\text{score} + \text{shortfall} = \text{pass}$" as a line before substituting anything.

### Income, expenditure and savings
Income $=$ expenditure $+$ savings. Take income as a friendly 100 units and the percents become the money itself.

| Item | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Income | 400 | $400 \times \dfrac{23}{20} = 460$ |
| Expenditure (80% of income) | 320 | $320 \times \dfrac{11}{10} = 352$ |
| Savings | 80 | $460 - 352 = 108$ |

Savings rose by $\dfrac{28}{80} \times 100 = 35\%$.

> **Watch:** The savings per cent is measured on the old savings (80), never on income.

### Price rises and consumption
Same budget, higher price, so the quantity must fall.

$$\text{quantity chip} = \frac{\text{budget chip}}{\text{price chip}}$$

Petrol price rises $25\%$: price chip $\dfrac{5}{4}$, budget chip 1, so quantity chip $= 1 \div \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{4}{5}$. Consumption must fall $20\%$.

> **Note:** A $25\%$ rise pairs with a $20\%$ cut. This is the more/less flip of the previous subtopic.

### A price cut and the extra quantity
Same money after a price cut buys more.

Price falls $20\%$: chip $\dfrac{4}{5}$. Quantity chip $= 1 \div \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{5}{4}$, a $25\%$ rise.

Worked: Rs 400 spent on rice. After a $20\%$ price cut, the same money buys 5 kg more.

1. Old price Rs $p$ per kg: old quantity $= \dfrac{400}{p}$.
2. New price $= 0.8p$; new quantity $= \dfrac{400}{0.8p} = \dfrac{500}{p}$.
3. Extra $= \dfrac{100}{p} = 5$, so $p = 20$.

> **Careful:** The extra quantity per cent is not the cut per cent. A $20\%$ cut buys $25\%$ more.

### Checking the direction
Every question in this subtopic is a chain of chips. Before answering, say the direction out loud: are you moving from old to new, or back?

- Marks: percents of $M$ move up to marks.
- Income: chips move income and expenditure forward, savings are the remainder.
- Prices: budget chip over price chip gives the quantity chip.

> **Example:** Income 400 rising $15\%$ is $400 \times \dfrac{23}{20} = 460$: multiply forward, never add 15% of something else.

patterns.name: Two candidates and the maximum marks
patterns.howToSpot: One candidate fails by some marks, another crosses the pass mark; maximum marks or the pass mark is asked.
steps: Note the two percents and the two distances from the pass mark.
Percent span = higher percent minus lower percent.
Maximum marks = marks span x 100 / percent span.
patterns.why: Both candidates' scores are percents of the same maximum, so their gap fixes it.

example.q: In an examination, A scores 33% and fails by 45 marks, while B scores 45% and gets 15 marks more than the pass mark. What are the maximum marks?

patterns.name: Income rise and the change in savings
patterns.howToSpot: Income and expenditure both change by percents; the effect on savings is asked.
steps: Assume a friendly income (say 400) and the expenditure percent.
Move income and expenditure forward with chips.
New savings = new income - new expenditure.
Compare with old savings for the per cent change.
patterns.why: Savings are just the remainder, so both chips flow into it.

example.q: A family earns Rs 400 a month and spends 80% of it. Income rises by 15% and expenditure rises by 10%. By what percentage do the savings increase?

patterns.name: Price rise, consumption cut
patterns.howToSpot: A price rises by a percent and the matching cut in consumption (same budget) is asked.
steps: State it as the cut needed.
patterns.why: With a fixed budget, quantity chip is one over the price chip.

example.q: The price of petrol rises by 25%. By what percentage must consumption be reduced to keep the expenditure unchanged?

patterns.name: Price cut and the extra quantity
patterns.howToSpot: A price falls by a percent; the same money now buys extra kilograms, and the price is asked.
steps: Write the quantity chip as one over the price chip.
Extra per cent = quantity chip minus 1.
Use the extra kilograms to find the old quantity.
Price = money divided by old quantity.
patterns.why: A fixed budget divided by a smaller price gives a bigger quantity, and the surplus pins the old quantity.

example.q: A household spends Rs 400 on rice every month. After a 20% fall in the price of rice, the same money buys 5 kg more. What was the original price per kg?
steps: Quantity chip $= \dfrac{5}{4}$, so extra $= \dfrac{1}{4}$ of old quantity $= 5$ kg.

patterns.name: One candidate and the pass mark
patterns.howToSpot: A single candidate's percent, the shortfall, and the pass mark are given; maximum marks is asked.
steps: Turn the shortfall into the candidate's marks: pass minus shortfall.
That equals x% of the maximum.
Divide and multiply by 100 for M.
patterns.why: One candidate's score is one percent slice of the maximum, so one equation is enough.

example.q: A student scores 30% in an examination and fails by 20 marks. If the pass mark is 152, what are the maximum marks?

revision: Pass $= x\%$ of $M + a$ when a candidate fails by $a$.
Savings change is measured on the old savings.
Price up $x\%$, same budget: consumption down $\dfrac{100x}{100+x}\%$.

pyqPatterns.approach:
Find 10% first (move the dot one place left).
Build your % from pieces of 10% and 5%.

example.q: What is 35% of 480?

pyqPatterns.pattern: Goes up by some %, then down
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A price or number rises, then falls (or the reverse). Asks the final change.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Start with 100.
Apply the changes one at a time.

example.q: Price rises 20%, then falls 20%. Net change?
example.solution:
Start: 100
Up 20% → 120
Down 20% of 120 (that is 24) → 96
100 became 96, so **4% less**

pyqPatterns.pattern: "A is more than B" — so B is less than A
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "A is 20% more than B. B is what % less than A?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Start with B = 100 and find A.
Compare the gap with A (the bigger one), not B.

example.q: A is 20% more than B. B is how much % less than A?
example.solution:
B = 100, so A = 120
Gap = 20
Gap out of A: 20 ÷ 120 = **16⅔% less**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Population changes by some % each year. Find the number after 2–3 years.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Do one year at a time.
Never add the % of different years.

example.q: Population 40,000. Up 10% in year 1, down 5% in year 2. Final?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Some votes are invalid. Winner's % and winning margin are given.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Use only the valid votes.
The winner's lead = gap between the two % × valid votes.

example.q: 20% of votes are invalid. Winner gets 60% of valid votes and wins by 1,200. Total votes?
example.solution:
Winner 60%, loser 40% → lead = 20% of valid votes
20% of valid = 1,200 → valid = 6,000
Valid is 80% of total → total = 6,000 ÷ 80 × 100 = **7,500**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One student fails by some marks, another passes with extra. Find full marks.
pyqPatterns.approach: The % gap between the two scores = the marks gap between them.

example.q: 33% fails by 45 marks. 45% gets 15 above pass marks. Full marks?
example.solution:
33% → 45% is a gap of 12%
Marks gap = 45 + 15 = 60
12% of full marks = 60 → full marks = 60 ÷ 12 × 100 = **500**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Price changes, so you buy more or less
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Price falls 20%, now you can buy 5 kg more for the same money."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Work out how much money the price cut saves.
That saved money buys the extra kg.

example.q: After a 20% price cut, ₹400 buys 5 kg more. Old price per kg?
example.solution:
Cut saves 20% of 400 = ₹80
₹80 buys 5 kg → new price = 80 ÷ 5 = ₹16
₹16 is 80% of old price → old = 16 ÷ 80 × 100 = **₹20**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Income and spending both rise. Asks how much savings change.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Start with income = 100.
Find new spending, then new savings.

example.q: Spends 80% of income. Income +15%, spending +10%. Savings up by what %?
example.solution:
Income 100, spends 80, saves 20
New income 115, new spending 88, saves 27
Savings rose 7 on 20 → **35%**

solvedExamples.q: A number is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net percentage change?
Find the value of $16\frac{2}{3}\%$ of 720 $+$ $33\frac{1}{3}\%$ of 450.
The price of an article is first increased by 10% and then decreased by 10%. What is the net change in price?
solvedExamples.solution:
Net $= 10 - 10 - \frac{10 \times 10}{100} = -1\%$.
A rise of 10% followed by a fall of 10% always leaves a **1% decrease**.

solvedExamples.q: A's salary is 25% more than B's salary. B's salary is what per cent less than A's salary?
The value of a machine depreciates at the rate of 10% per annum. If its present value is ₹8,100, what was its value 2 years ago?
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the value 2 years ago be P.
$P\left(\frac{90}{100}\right)^2 = 8100$
$P \times \frac{81}{100} = 8100$, so P = ₹10,000.

$0.2 \times 0.8T = 1200$ ⇒ $0.16T = 1200$ ⇒ T = 7500.

practice.solution:
Consumption factor $= \frac{\text{expenditure factor}}{\text{price factor}} = \frac{108}{120} = \frac{9}{10}$.
So consumption must be cut by **10%**.
practice.shortcut: 1.08 ÷ 1.20 = 0.90 ⇒ reduce 10%. (20% is the trap from the standard 'same expenditure' rule.)

Take income = 100 ⇒ expenditure = 80, savings = 20.
New income = 115, new expenditure = 88 ⇒ new savings = 27.
Increase $= \frac{7}{20} \times 100 = 35\%$.
practice.shortcut: Track the three quantities on income = 100. Savings go 20 → 27 = +35%.

practice.solution:
Money saved due to the cut = 20% of ₹400 = ₹80.
This ₹80 buys the extra 5 kg at the reduced price ⇒ reduced price = ₹16/kg.
Original price = ₹$16 \times \frac{100}{80}$ = ₹20 per kg.
practice.shortcut: r% of outlay ÷ extra kg = reduced price (80/5 = 16); original = reduced ÷ 0.8 = 20.

practice.solution:

(The question compares A with B — B is the base. 80% would be B as a % of A.)

practice.q: Two numbers are respectively 20% and 50% more than a third number. The first number is what per cent of the second number?
practice.solution:
Let the third number be 100 → the numbers are 120 and 150.
$\frac{120}{150} \times 100 = 80\%$.
practice.shortcut: Setting the third number to 100 kills the algebra — always do this.

Net $= -\frac{25^2}{100} = -6.25\%$ — order does not matter.

practice.q: After an increase of 20%, the population of a town is 8,400. What was the population before the increase?
After a reduction of 12.5% in its price, a gadget costs ₹3,500. What was its original price?
practice.shortcut: ₹3,937.50 comes from adding 12.5% back — wrong base again.

practice.q: The numerator of a fraction is increased by 50% and the denominator is decreased by 25%. As a result, the fraction:
practice.solution:
Numerator chip $\frac{3}{2}$, denominator chip $\frac{3}{4}$.
New factor $= \frac{3/2}{3/4} = 2$ → the fraction is doubled, i.e. a $100\%$ increase.

practice.q: The numerator of a fraction is decreased by 10% and the denominator is decreased by 20%. The fraction becomes:
practice.solution:
Chips: $\frac{9}{10}$ and $\frac{8}{10}$ → factor $= \frac{9/10}{8/10} = \frac{9}{8} = 1.125$.
The fraction increases by $12.5\%$.

practice.q: A number, when successively decreased by 10% and 20%, becomes 720. The original number is:
A quantity is increased by 10%, then by 20%, and the result is decreased by 25%. The net change in the quantity is:

practice.solution:
Let B = 100 → A = 160. Gap = 60, base = 160.
$\frac{60}{160} \times 100 = 37.5\%$. (60% is the trap — wrong base.)

practice.q: The price of a car is 50% more than that of a bike. The price of the bike is what per cent less than that of the car?

In an office, 40% of the employees are graduates and 25% of the graduates are post-graduates. What per cent of the total employees are post-graduates?
practice.solution:
$\frac{40}{100} \times \frac{25}{100} = \frac{10}{100}$ → 10%.
(65% adds percentages on different bases — the classic trap.)

practice.q: A's height is $16\frac{2}{3}\%$ more than B's height. B's height is what per cent less than A's height?
practice.solution:
$16\frac{2}{3}\% = \frac{1}{6}$ → A : B = 7 : 6.
B is less by $\frac{1}{7} = 14\frac{2}{7}\%$ of A's height.

practice.solution:
A = 100 → B = 25. Gap = 75 on base 25 → $\frac{75}{25} \times 100 = 300\%$.
(400% would answer 'A is what % of B'.)

practice.shortcut: Take C = 100 → B = 20 → A = 5, same result.

practice.solution: Required rise $= 300$ units on the reduced base 1,200 → $\frac{300}{1200} \times 100 = 25\%$.

practice.solution: $96000 \times \frac{5}{4} \times \frac{4}{5} = 96{,}000$ — the chips are reciprocals, so the town is back where it started.

practice.q: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 55% of the valid votes and won by 2,700 votes. The number of valid votes polled was:
practice.solution:
Shares: 55% vs 45% → margin = 10% of valid votes.
$0.10 \times V = 2700$ → V = 27,000.

practice.q: In an election between two candidates, 15% of the total votes polled were invalid. The winner got 60% of the valid votes and won by 2,040 votes. The total number of votes polled was:
practice.solution:
Valid = 85% of polled. Winner 60%, loser 40% → margin = 20% of valid.
Valid $= \frac{2040}{0.20} = 10{,}200$ → polled $= \frac{10200}{0.85} = 12{,}000$.

practice.q: In an examination, a candidate scoring 40% of the maximum marks fails by 20 marks, while another candidate scoring 50% gets 30 marks more than the pass marks. The maximum marks are:
practice.solution:
Pass mark from A: $0.40M + 20$; from B: $0.50M - 30$.
$10\%$ of M $= 50$ → M $= 500$. Pass mark $= 220$ (both agree).

practice.q: In an examination, a candidate scoring 30% of the maximum marks fails by 25 marks. If the pass mark is 175, the maximum marks are:
A person spends 80% of his income. His income increases by 15% and his expenditure increases by 10%. His savings increase by:
practice.solution:
Income = 100 → spends 80, saves 20.
New: income 115, expenditure 88 → savings 27.
Increase $= \frac{7}{20} \times 100 = 35\%$.

practice.q: Ravi saves 25% of his income. His income rises by 30% and his expenditure rises by 20%. His new savings are what per cent more than his earlier savings?
practice.solution:
Income = 100 → saves 25, spends 75.
New: income 130, expenditure 90 → savings 40.
Increase $= \frac{15}{25} \times 100 = 60\%$.
